items.title: Alibaba shares plunge 11% after $10.2 billion share placement to fund AI expansion
items.one_liner: Alibaba shares dropped 11% following a $10.2 billion share placement intended to aggressively fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure.
items.summary: Alibaba shares plunged up to 11% on Monday after announcing an HK$80 billion ($10.2 billion) share placement to fund its artificial intelligence expansion. The Chinese technology major plans to issue 710 million new shares at HK$112.70 each, below the previous close of HK$123, with proceeds dedicated to strengthening full-stack AI capabilities and infrastructure. This capital raise follows a 75% year-on-year drop in June-quarter net profit due to elevated spending on AI and computing infrastructure.

items.bottom_line: Alibaba's massive $10.2 billion share placement for AI investments has triggered immediate stock dilution fears and an 11% share price plunge.

items.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
items.one_liner: An actively exploited Oracle access control flaw has been added to the KEV catalog, requiring immediate patching for those managing WebLogic or HTTP server infrastructure.
items.summary: CISA has added a critical Oracle vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog following evidence of active exploitation. The flaw, CVE-2026-21962, affects Oracle HTTP Server and Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-ins, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to bypass access controls. Federal agencies are required to prioritize remediation of this vulnerability under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. CISA strongly encourages all private sector organizations to patch this flaw immediately to prevent total asset compromise.
key_facts: CVE-2026-21962: Improper Access Control in Oracle HTTP/WebLogic
Affected Products: Oracle HTTP Server, Oracle Weblogic Server Proxy Plug-in
items.bottom_line: Organizations must prioritize patching CVE-2026-21962 to prevent unauthenticated attackers from gaining total control over Oracle-based web infrastructure.

items.title: Vibe Coding and Web Application Security: A Twin-Prompt Study
items.one_liner: Practical evidence that security prompting is a mandatory step for developers using AI coding assistants.
items.summary: A study on vibe coding—generating entire web applications from natural language prompts—investigated whether adding security requirements to prompts improves code safety. Researchers compared baseline prompts against security-aware variants for six different applications. The security-aware prompts resulted in significantly fewer vulnerabilities (24 vs. 51) and eliminated all Critical or High severity issues. While the study is preliminary and used a small sample, it suggests that explicit security instructions in agentic coding workflows are highly effective.
items.bottom_line: Explicitly including security requirements in LLM prompts drastically reduces the number and severity of vulnerabilities in generated code.

claims.text: Security-aware prompts reduced confirmed findings from 51 to 24.
claims.support_span: The security-aware variant produced fewer confirmed findings in every application (24 versus 51) and contained no Critical or High issues

claims.text: The study used six functionally distinct web applications.
claims.support_span: We study six functionally distinct web applications, each generated in two prompt variants that are identical except for an appended security-requirements section

items.title: ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat
items.one_liner: A high-risk Android threat that uses developer features to bypass security and steal corporate credentials.
items.summary: The ToxicPanda Android banking Trojan has evolved into version 2.0, significantly expanding its target list from 16 to 349 financial applications. The malware now uses Android's Wireless Debugging and Accessibility Services to gain shell-level access and escalate privileges without a physical connection. It features lock-screen overlays to steal credentials and leverages AWS infrastructure for distribution. This version poses a direct threat to enterprises as it can compromise devices used for MFA and corporate resource access.
items.bottom_line: ToxicPanda 2.0 has transitioned from a simple banking Trojan to a sophisticated tool for full device compromise and enterprise identity theft.

items.title: Microsoft Patches Severe Entra ID Flaw (CVSS 10.0) Allowing Remote Code Execution
items.one_liner: A CVSS 10.0 RCE in Entra ID has been mitigated by Microsoft; while no user action is needed, it underscores the critical nature of cloud identity infrastructure security.
items.summary: Microsoft has patched a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Entra ID, tracked as CVE-2026-69836 with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0. The flaw stemmed from the deserialization of untrusted data, which could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. Although initially reported as exploited in the wild, Microsoft later corrected the status to indicate no active exploitation has been observed. Because Entra ID is a cloud-based service, Microsoft has already applied the mitigation, and no customer action is required.
key_facts: Affected Service: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD)
Vulnerability Type: Deserialization of untrusted data
items.bottom_line: Microsoft has fully mitigated a maximum-severity RCE flaw in Entra ID, and users do not need to take any manual action to secure their environments.

claims.text: Microsoft corrected the status of CVE-2026-69836 to not exploited.
claims.support_span: on August 21, 2026, Microsoft corrected the "Exploited" status to "No" after The Hacker News contacted the company for comment.

items.summary: Healthcare technology provider CareCloud confirmed a massive data breach affecting over 3.75 million individuals, significantly higher than the initial estimate of 345,000. items.title: When Retrieval Fails Before It Begins: Structurally Indirect Prerequisite Eviction as a Retention Failure in Agentic Memory
items.one_liner: Implement graph-aware dependency rules like DSGC in your agent memory systems to prevent critical upstream context from being prematurely evicted.
items.summary: Researchers have identified a pre-retrieval failure mode in agentic memory systems under fixed token budgets called structurally indirect prerequisite eviction, where upstream execution blocks weakly aligned with a query are mistakenly discarded. To address this, they evaluated Dependency-aware Semantic Garbage Collection (DSGC), a one-hop graph-aware rule that ensures crucial prerequisite context survives budget pressure. In their main evaluation suite, DSGC significantly improved full-chain retention from 0.03 to 0.90 under a lexical encoder and from 0.23 to 1.00 under a sentence encoder. The findings demonstrate that memory failures often occur before retrieval due to improper retention mechanics.

Sentence encoder retention improvement: From 0.23 to 1.00
items.bottom_line: Agent memory failures often happen before retrieval due to budget-driven prerequisite eviction, which can be mitigated using graph-aware dependency collection rules.

items.title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Jailbreak Beyond Textual Jailbreak in Hidden-State Risk Space
items.one_liner: PRISM uses hidden-state logistic probing to detect physical jailbreak risks in LLM agent planners without high false-positive rates.
items.summary: Large language models acting as high-level planners for embodied or agentic systems can receive linguistically benign instructions that become unsafe when grounded in the physical world. The authors study whether this physical jailbreak is distinct from textual jailbreak, showing through hidden-state analysis that they form separable signals across multiple model families. To detect physical safety risks without high false-positive rates from standard LLM judges, they propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. Tested on SafeAgentBench and an interaction-balanced revision of PhysicalJailbreakBench-2K, PRISM outperforms LLM judges by achieving strong balanced accuracy with significantly lower false-positive rates.
items.bottom_line: Physical safety violations in LLM planners can be accurately detected via hidden-state representation probes, bypassing the high false-positive rates of text-level moderators.

claims.text: Building on this separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states.

items.title: Trustworthy RAG: An Evaluation Agent for Detecting Misinformation and Knowledge Poisoning in Generative AI Systems
items.one_liner: An evaluation agent middleware combines NLI verification and a Trust Index to block knowledge poisoning and instruction injections in RAG systems.
items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems typically trust retrieved text blindly, creating a security gap where high semantic relevance masks poisoned or malicious content. To counter this, researchers propose an Evaluation Agent that combines Natural Language Inference factual verification, a five-signal poison detector, and a Trust Index with a non-linear dampener. Tested on TruthfulQA with Llama 3.3 70B, the agent achieved 91% accuracy, 100% precision, and 100% recall on instruction injection, though in-place entity swaps remain difficult to catch. In a secure-coding task utilizing OWASP Top 10 and CWE guidance, the agent blocked unsafe instructions with an F1 score of 92%.
items.bottom_line: RAG pipelines can be effectively shielded from knowledge poisoning before generation using a multi-signal evaluation middleware rather than trusting retrieved content.

items.title: aiXamine: Unified Black-Box Evaluation of Cross-Dimensional Trade-offs in LLM Safety, Security, and Privacy
items.one_liner: aiXamine reveals critical cross-dimensional trade-offs in LLM safety, security, and privacy through unified black-box evaluation.
items.summary: Large language models often suffer from cross-dimensional failures where optimizations in safety alignment degrade utility, security, or privacy properties. The authors introduce aiXamine, a unified black-box evaluation platform that orchestrates 46 tests across nine services to assess trustworthiness dimensions jointly. Evaluating over 120 LLMs through more than 5,000 test runs, the study uncovers three major phenomena: a safety tax where strict alignment increases over-refusals, near-orthogonality between privacy and other metrics, and distillation-induced robustness collapse where off-policy distillation catastrophically destroys robustness. These results prove that trustworthiness properties are interdependent and cannot be reliably evaluated in isolation.
items.bottom_line: Evaluating LLMs across isolated safety, security, or privacy axes misses critical trade-offs like the safety tax and distillation-induced robustness collapse.

claims.text: Applying aiXamine to over 120 LLMs through more than 5,000 test runs, we conduct the largest joint safety, security, and privacy study to date and uncover three cross-dimensional phenomena invisible to single-axis evaluation.
claims.support_span: Applying aiXamine to over 120 LLMs through more than 5,000 test runs, we conduct the largest joint safety, security, and privacy study to date and uncover three cross-dimensional phenomena invisible to single-axis evaluation.

items.title: Utility Under Attack: Agent Memory Poisoning and the Limits of Content Screening and Provenance Ranking
items.one_liner: Agent memory poisoning severely degrades LLM accuracy, and content-only screening or provenance weighting fails to block it effectively.
items.summary: Persistent memory allows false information to endure across agent sessions, significantly degrading system accuracy when poisoned. Testing a LongMemEval corpus, researchers found that poisoning just 1.2% of entries drops model accuracy from 0.850 to 0.300, while a standard write-time content-screening pipeline failed to reject any of the poisoned memories. Content-only screening proves insufficient because distinguishing false assertions from true ones requires external grounding. Furthermore, provenance-weighted retrieval methods fail to provide a useful setting under standard similarity regimes, as weights strong enough to block query-shaped poison also suppress legitimate untrusted evidence. The authors advocate for bounded occupancy constraints at retrieval instead of additive provenance penalties.
items.bottom_line: Protecting AI agent memory from poisoning requires bounded occupancy constraints at retrieval rather than relying on failing content screening or additive provenance weights.

claims.text: Poisoning 1.2% of a LongMemEval corpus reduces accuracy from 0.850 to 0.300.
claims.support_span: Poisoning 1.2% of a LongMemEval corpus reduces accuracy from 0.850 to 0.300.

items.title: Automated Trajectory Evaluation for Mobile Agents via Step-Level Consequence Reasoning and Aggregation
items.one_liner: CRATE uses step-level consequence reasoning in vision-language models to automate mobile agent evaluation and operational safety assessments.
items.summary: Evaluating language-guided mobile agents has shifted toward model-based judges, but holistic evaluation of entire trajectories causes context overload and overlooks operational safety. To solve this, researchers introduce CRATE, a two-stage vision-language model judge framework that uses step-level consequence reasoning to independently extract visual clues and action-conditioned state changes before aggregating them for evaluation. An extension, CRATE-S, handles operational safety assessments. Powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct, CRATE achieved an F1 score of 0.833 on AndroidWorld—outperforming SPA-Bench by 20%—while CRATE-S reached an F1 score of 0.697 on MobileRisk.
items.bottom_line: Step-level consequence reasoning in VLM judges dramatically improves the accuracy and safety evaluation of mobile AI agents compared to holistic trajectory grading.

claims.text: Powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct, CRATE achieves an F1-score of 0.833 on AndroidWorld (outperforming SPA-Bench by 20%), while CRATE-S reaches an F1-score of 0.697 on MobileRisk, demonstrating strong alignment with benchmark ground truths.

items.title: BackDFL: A Unified Benchmark For Backdoor Attacks and Defenses In Decentralized Federated Learning
items.one_liner: BackDFL is a unified benchmark that exposes the vulnerability of decentralized federated learning to backdoor attacks at low participation rates.
items.summary: Decentralized Federated Learning removes the centralized parameter server in favor of peer-to-peer model exchange, but this shift increases susceptibility to backdoor attacks where malicious participants embed hidden behaviors while maintaining clean performance. This paper argues that DFL robustness has been overestimated due to fragmented evaluation protocols and non-adaptive adversaries. To address this, the authors present BackDFL, a unified benchmark for evaluating DFL under realistic and adaptive backdoor attacks. Experiments with BackDFL demonstrate that existing Byzantine-robust DFL methods and adapted FL backdoor defenses fail under malicious participation rates as low as 15%, particularly in heterogeneous settings across varying network topologies.
key_facts: Malicious participation rate threshold: as low as 15%
items.bottom_line: Decentralized federated learning systems fail under modest malicious participation rates of 15%, exposing significant gaps in current Byzantine-robust defenses.

claims.text: Our results demonstrate that both state-of-the-art Byzantine-robust DFL methods and adapted FL backdoor defenses fail under modest malicious participation rates (as low as 15%), especially in heterogeneous settings, while their robustness varies substantially across communication graph topologies.
claims.support_span: Our results demonstrate that both state-of-the-art Byzantine-robust DFL methods and adapted FL backdoor defenses fail under modest malicious participation rates (as low as 15%), especially in heterogeneous settings, while their robustness varies substantially across communication graph topologies.

items.title: SIREN (Luring LLMs onto the Rocks): PAIR-Driven Preference Manipulation in Web-RAG Recommenders
items.one_liner: The SIREN framework uses PAIR-driven preference manipulation to force poisoned web sources into top ranks in web-augmented LLMs.
items.summary: This paper explores the adversarial manipulation of ranked recommendations generated by web-augmented large language models that read live web pages. The authors introduce SIREN, an automated attacker-judge method adapting the PAIR jailbreaking loop to competitive rank manipulation by iteratively editing retrieved source content using an interpretable taxonomy of 23 poisoning techniques. Testing across production Claude models via a custom RAG replay platform that keeps the surrounding source set fixed, SIREN achieved rank 1 in 62 out of 124 technique trials. Payloads that reached top ranking successfully reproduced the result in fresh sessions with a mean success rate of 0.805, demonstrating the severe vulnerability of web-RAG recommendation engines to subtle source edits.
items.bottom_line: Web-RAG recommendation engines can be reliably manipulated to promote targeted entities to top ranks through subtle, localized content poisoning of retrieved web pages.

items.title: Certified Multi-Turn Robustness for LLM Safety via Compositional Bounds and Safety Persistence
items.one_liner: Multi-Turn Certified Robustness models conversational safety as State-Adversarial MDPs to provide tighter safety bounds against multi-turn jailbreaks.
items.summary: Large language models are vulnerable to multi-turn jailbreak attacks that gradually manipulate conversational context, while existing certified robustness methods degrade exponentially when applied across multiple turns. To fix this, researchers introduce Multi-Turn Certified Robustness, a framework that models conversational safety via State-Adversarial Markov Decision Processes. The framework features compositional certification via embedding-space mode decomposition and (alpha, beta)-safety persistence, improving degradation rates from exponential multiplication to bounded persistence. Experiments across six LLMs under bounded and Crescendo-style attacks confirm that empirical safety consistently exceeds the theoretical certified bounds.
items.bottom_line: Multi-turn LLM jailbreaks can be bounded effectively using State-Adversarial MDP modeling and safety persistence frameworks rather than naive exponential composition.

claims.text: We introduce Multi-Turn Certified Robustness (MTCR), a framework that models conversational safety via State-Adversarial MDPs and defines $k$-turn certified robustness as the worst-case safety probability across $k$ adversarial turns.
claims.support_span: We introduce Multi-Turn Certified Robustness (MTCR), a framework that models conversational safety via State-Adversarial MDPs and defines $k$-turn certified robustness as the worst-case safety probability across $k$ adversarial turns.

items.title: MalSkills: Detecting Malicious Skills in the Agentic Supply Chain via Neuro-symbolic Reasoning
items.one_liner: This research highlights a new frontier in supply-chain security: the risk of malicious 'skills' or modules in LLM agent marketplaces.
items.summary: MalSkills is a neuro-symbolic framework designed to detect malicious skills in the agentic supply chain by combining symbolic parsing with LLM-assisted semantic analysis. It constructs a skill dependency graph to track value flows and operations, then uses reasoning to identify suspicious patterns. In a study of over 150,000 skills from public registries, MalSkills flagged 620 potentially malicious items, 400 of which were manually confirmed as malicious. The framework achieved a 93% F1 score, significantly outperforming existing static and dynamic detection methods.
items.bottom_line: MalSkills demonstrates that the agentic supply chain is already being targeted by malicious actors and provides a scalable way to detect these threats.

items.title: GitLab CVE-2026-19478 Comes Under Active Exploitation Within Days of Disclosure
items.one_liner: An unauthenticated GitLab code injection flaw is under active exploitation, allowing attackers to manipulate public repositories and forge development history.
items.summary: A critical code injection vulnerability in GitLab, CVE-2026-19478 (CVSS 9.4), is being actively exploited just days after its disclosure. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to modify or delete public projects, forge merge records, and ban maintainers via a GraphQL directive. items.one_liner: The ChainDrop worm's ability to backdoor VS Code and Claude Code directly impacts developers using AI-assisted tooling and modern CI/CD pipelines.
items.summary: The ChainDrop npm worm has infected over 400 packages, targeting developer environments and CI/CD pipelines to steal credentials and self-propagate. By establishing persistence in these tools, attackers maintain access even after a build completes. The worm manages its command-and-control infrastructure via Ethereum blockchain transactions, making it highly resilient to traditional takedowns.

items.bottom_line: Attackers are now backdooring developer tools like VS Code and Claude Code to maintain persistent access to the software supply chain.

items.title: I Changed One “User_Id” and the API Said “Sure” — From Password Reset to Mass Account Takeover
items.one_liner: An API password-reset endpoint allowed unauthenticated mass account takeover simply by modifying the user ID parameter in the request body.
items.summary: During an authorized API penetration test, a researcher discovered a critical mass account takeover vulnerability within a password-reset endpoint. The backend API trusted client-supplied JSON parameters—specifically the User_Id field—without verifying authorization, session tokens, current passwords, or OTPs. The flaw highlights the severe risks of client-side trust in sensitive authentication workflows.
items.bottom_line: Failing to validate server-side session authorization against user identifiers in password reset APIs allows full account compromise.

items.title: Critical Keycloak Password Reset Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Take Over Any Account
items.one_liner: A critical Keycloak flaw allows unauthenticated account takeover by bypassing password reset tokens, requiring immediate updates for identity management servers.
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in Keycloak, tracked as CVE-2026-18963 with a CVSS score of 9.1, allows unauthenticated attackers to take over any user account, including administrative ones. The flaw is caused by improper state validation in the password reset flow, enabling an attacker to bypass the required email action token and transition directly to the password update phase. Red Hat has released patches for both upstream Keycloak and the Red Hat build of Keycloak (RHBK). Organizations unable to patch immediately are advised to disable the 'Forgot password' functionality across all realms as a temporary mitigation.
key_facts: Affected Versions: Keycloak versions prior to 26.7.2
Mitigation: Disable 'Forgot password' in Realm settings
items.bottom_line: Unauthenticated attackers can seize any Keycloak account by exploiting a flaw in the password reset mechanism; immediate patching or disabling the 'Forgot password' feature is required.
